labs.title: CIS-2: the same AI output, bit for bit, on different machines
labs.hard_question: Can two different computers produce the exact same AI output, bit for bit, from a written specification?
labs.method: Spec v0.3b pins the arithmetic (reduction order, no FMA, FTZ/DAZ, pinned polynomials, RoPE table); a SHA-256 witness chain over the full logits is the receipt. Public conformance vectors on Hugging Face. Pinned vector: SmolLM2-135M, prompt 'Once upon a time', 16 greedy tokens, fp32. The 9-check selfcheck.sh was run by the maintainer on own x86_64 machines (AVX2 and scalar; README machine table). On a free Lightning AI Studio (Xeon Platinum 8488C, 4 vCPU, AVX-512 flags, gcc 13.3.0, Ubuntu 24.04) only the narrower scripts/self_check.sh (four digests) was run, not selfcheck.sh. An aarch64 Android phone reproduced the pinned digests through the KV-cache verify3 path, not the self-check script. Run by us.

results.claim: A free Lightning AI cloud Studio (Xeon Platinum 8488C, CPU not owned by us) matched all four pinned digests using the narrower scripts/self_check.sh, not the 9-check selfcheck.sh. Driven by the maintainer.
results.quote: **Result: PASS — all four digests match the pinned test vector.**

results.claim: The README's documented expected selfcheck.sh output (shown with an i5-5200U fingerprint, the box1 AVX2 row) ends in 9 passed, 0 failed. This is shown as expected output; the machine table separately lists box1 with its log not published.
results.quote: == SUMMARY: 9 passed, 0 failed ==

results.claim: The aarch64 Android phone reproduced the pinned digests through a different code path; the self-check script itself was not run on it.
results.quote: `selfcheck.sh` not run on the device; the pinned §13.1 digests were reproduced on it through the KV-cache `verify3/` path

caveats: Run by us on every machine, including the cloud workspace; the README says: No unaffiliated party has reproduced it yet.
One model (SmolLM2-135M), one prompt, 16 tokens, fp32 greedy decoding only (no sampling, batching or quantization), mostly CPU; production bf16/GPU serving is outside the spec today.
Full logs for most machine-table rows are published as 'log not published'.

The Lightning run used scripts/self_check.sh (four digests), not the 9-check selfcheck.sh; the 9-passed line is the README's expected-output block (i5-5200U fingerprint), not a separately published log.
The Lightning Studio is a free tier workspace, not a rented one; no timing numbers reported.
One machine-table host (penguin) had weights copied over the LAN because its resolver could not reach the Hugging Face CDN; the pinned sha256 of all three artifacts was still verified.

labs.learned: With the arithmetic pinned in writing, one fp32 digest reproduced across AVX2 and scalar x86, an aarch64 phone and an AVX-512-capable cloud CPU (generic build, self-check only), in our own runs. Until an outsider runs it, the claim stays 'reproduced by us'.

explainer.question: Can different computers produce exactly the same AI output, bit for bit, from a written specification?
explainer.why: If the same AI gives different bits on different machines, nobody can check a result by re-running it. A spec that makes the bits identical turns 'trust us' into 'run it yourself'.
steps: Write the arithmetic down: order of additions, no fused multiply-add, fixed sin/cos formulas.
Pin one test: SmolLM2-135M, the prompt 'Once upon a time', 16 tokens, fp32.
Hash the full output scores into a SHA-256 chain. That digest is the receipt.
Run the self-check on other machines and compare with the pinned digests.
explainer.headline: 4 of 4 digests match
explainer.result: A free cloud machine (Xeon Platinum 8488C, not ours) matched all four pinned digests. An Android phone matched them through a different code path. The README's expected self-check output ends 9 passed, 0 failed.
explainer.meaning: With the arithmetic pinned, the bits reproduced across these machines in our own runs. It says nothing about whether the model is right, safe or fair, and no outside party has reproduced it yet.
explainer.analogy: Like a recipe that fixes the oven settings and the order of every step, so every oven bakes the same cake, crumb for crumb.

results.quote: **Status: PASS. Run of 2026-09-08 12:07 UTC, NVIDIA Tesla P100-PCIE-16GB (sm_60, Pascal), CUDA 12.8.**

results.claim: Two earlier GPU runs were false positives (the binary was really built for the CPU) and are withdrawn.
results.quote: Earlier attempts v6 and v7 were **false positives** and are withdrawn

caveats: One GPU generation (Pascal), one driver and compiler, one model (SmolLM2-135M), one prompt, horizon up to 128 tokens.
Correctness only: no performance or timing claim; no tensor-core, batched, multi-stream or multi-GPU paths; nothing about Ampere, Hopper or Blackwell.

Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.

explainer.question: Does the same AI output come out bit for bit on a graphics card, not just on other CPUs?
explainer.why: Most AI runs on graphics cards. A claim that only holds on CPUs would miss where the work is done.
steps: Write an independent CUDA version of the same spec.
Run the four test vectors on a Kaggle Tesla P100 with the internet off.
Compare the GPU digests with the CPU digests.
Sample GPU use and read the compiled code to prove the work ran on the GPU.
explainer.headline: 4 of 4 vectors match
explainer.result: All four vectors matched the CPU digests on the GPU (Tesla P100, run of 2026-09-08). Two earlier GPU runs were false positives, because the program had really been built for the CPU, and we withdrew them.
explainer.meaning: The bits reproduce on one older GPU generation. It says nothing about speed or newer GPUs, and our CUDA code is not public, so outsiders cannot rerun our port.

labs.title: Batching and precision on a Tesla T4: which shortcuts change the digest
labs.hard_question: Do common GPU speed shortcuts, like batching requests or switching to int8, quietly change the answer?
labs.method: One matmul (q_proj, layer 0, hidden size 576) of the reference model on a Kaggle Tesla T4 (sm_75) and a host CPU build (g++; CUDA build via nvcc for sm_75): row-batched fp32, grouped fp32 and int8 at batch sizes 1, 4 and 8, plus a batch-1 host control (10 configurations). Diffs are counted over 576 output elements against the batch-1 CPU reference. Run by us; driver source and recipe not published. No timing figures are reported.

results.claim: Row-batched fp32 matched the batch-1 reference exactly at every batch size, on host and GPU.
results.quote: fp32-seq matched the batch=1 reference exactly at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 (0/576 diffs each), on both the host build and the T4 CUDA build.

results.claim: Grouped fp32 and int8 changed the result at every batch size tested, as the report predicted before the run (455/576 and 576/576 differing elements respectively).
results.quote: fp32-grouped and int8 mismatched at every batch size tested (455/576 and 576/576 diffs respectively)

results.claim: Host and CUDA builds agreed on all 10 configurations.
results.quote: Host and CUDA builds produced bit-identical digests for every one of the 10

caveats: Single matmul (q_proj, layer 0), not a full forward pass; the whole-model follow-on covers only row-batched fp32 and is in an internal log, not a public report.
One GPU architecture (Tesla T4, sm_75); no claim about other GPUs or compute capabilities.
Whether grouped or int8 could be made to match was not attempted; those mismatches were the expected outcome.
Driver source and Kaggle recipe not published, so the sweep cannot be re-run from public material.
The published sweep table lists host-build digests; the CUDA digests are reported as byte-identical to them, not tabulated separately.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
labs.learned: In our fp32 test, the pinned order of operations decided the digest. The same order matched on CPU and GPU, and a different order broke it, which is what a digest is supposed to detect. This is one matmul on one GPU type, so it shows the check works there, not that it holds everywhere.

explainer.question: Do common GPU speed shortcuts, like batching requests or switching to int8, quietly change the answer?
explainer.why: Batching and lower precision are the usual ways to make serving cheaper. If they silently change answers, a receipt has to be able to tell.
steps: Take one matrix multiply from the model (layer 0, q_proj).
Compute it on a Tesla T4 and a CPU three ways: row-batched fp32, grouped fp32, int8; batch sizes 1, 4, 8.
Count how many of the 576 output values differ from the batch-1 CPU answer.
Compare CPU and GPU digests across all 10 configurations.
explainer.headline: Row-batched: 0 of 576 differ
explainer.result: Row-batched fp32 matched the reference exactly at every batch size, on CPU and GPU. Grouped fp32 and int8 changed the result at every batch size (455 and 576 of 576 differ), as predicted before the run. CPU and GPU digests agreed on all 10.
explainer.meaning: The pinned order of operations decided the digest, which is what a digest should detect. One matrix multiply on one GPU type, so it shows the check works there, not everywhere.

labs.title: Clean-room reimplementations: one mismatch (from a memo), one match (from spec v0.1), one partial that exposed a spec error

results.claim: Second Rust attempt (E15g, spec v0.1 only) matched all four digests and all 16 token ids on x86_64 and aarch64 on its first CI run. The CI run is private.

results.claim: The E15g implementer read only the v0.1 spec text for algorithm content. It also read build and CI scaffolding files, which are logged.

results.quote: Result: PARTIAL conformance — 3 of 4 digests match bit-for-bit, cross-ISA/cross-compiler-identical

results.quote: root cause found — witness-chain item ORDER, not the forward pass

results.quote: copied verbatim from `docs/CIS2_SPEC_v0.2.md` §12.1's written prose

results.claim: After we corrected the spec and the C code, all four C cells reproduced the pinned CIS2_REF. We corrected the spec ourselves after seeing the mismatch, so this is a post-fix match.
results.quote:
E15j is now a full
4/4-digest, cross-language (Rust vs from-spec-text-only C11), cross-ISA

explainer.question: Can someone who has never seen our code build the same bits from the written description alone?
explainer.why: A specification is only useful if someone who never saw the original code can build the same thing from it.
steps: Give isolated AI coding agents the written material only, never our source code.
Three attempts: Rust from an internal memo, Rust from spec v0.1, C11 from spec v0.2.
Compare four digests and 16 token ids with the reference on x86_64 and aarch64.
When the C version missed one digest, hash every tensor and find where they first differ.
explainer.headline: 1 miss, 1 match, 1 partial
explainer.result: The memo-based build did not match. The spec v0.1 build matched all four digests and 16 token ids on its first run. The C11 build matched 3 of 4; the miss traced to our own spec text listing the digest-chain items in the wrong order. After we fixed the spec, it matched 4 of 4.
explainer.meaning: A written description can be enough, and a failed attempt exposed a real bug in our spec. But the builders were AI agents run by one operator inside our organisation, and the cited CI runs are private.
explainer.analogy: Like handing a recipe to a cook who has never seen your kitchen: when the dish comes out slightly off, the typo turns out to be in the recipe.

labs.title: Sin/cos accuracy for RoPE against a pre-registered 2 ULP bar (v0.2, v0.3, v0.3b)
labs.hard_question: Is the pinned sin/cos accurate enough for long contexts, measured against a bar we set before we tested?
labs.method: A pre-registration set a 2 ULP bar (oracle within 2 ULP of correctly-rounded f32) before the v0.3 fix was implemented. An mpmath 60-digit oracle covered RoPE angles for positions up to max_position_embeddings=8192, using the SmolLM2-135M (theta=1e5) and Qwen2.5-0.5B (theta=1e6) values. It compared three versions of the sin/cos reduction. The v0.3b mechanism was added by a coordinator directive after v0.3 missed the bar. Local x86_64 sandbox harness (scripts/h2m_accuracy_harness.py). Run by us.

results.claim: The pre-registration was written before implementation.
results.quote: **Status: pre-registered before implementation.**

results.claim: v0.2 (f32-only reduction, Taylor polynomial) had errors up to 115198 ULP for sin and up to 163969 ULP for cos, in the local oracle run.
results.quote: | v0.2 (f32-only reduce, Taylor) | up to 115198 | 1.30e-2 | up to 163969 | 1.36e-2 |

results.claim: v0.3 (f64-staged reduction only) cut the error by roughly 55 to 70 times, with a max of 2813.5 raw ULP, and still missed the 2 ULP bar. The doc attributes the residual to the unchanged Taylor polynomial.
results.quote: "<=2 ULP" bar is NOT met

results.claim: v0.3b (octant reduction plus separate minimax polynomials) reached a maximum of 1.5 ULP for sin and cos on both models and met the bar, in the local harness run.

caveats: Local x86_64 sandbox harness numbers only. CI runs were dispatched but were still in flight when the document was written, and the doc records no CI confirmation. Cross-ISA (aarch64) confirmation was pending.
Positions 0 to 8192 only. The v0.3b run used a dense grid (stride 7, plus positions 0 to 19 and the last position), not every position.
The 2 ULP bar was pre-registered for the v0.3 mechanism. The v0.3b mechanism was chosen after v0.3 missed, so it was not itself pre-registered.
The doc says the v0.3 ULP counts are inflated near sin/cos zero-crossings, a known property of the ULP metric. The v0.3 filtered figure (values with |sin/cos| >= 1e-2) is up to 486.5 ULP.
The work sits on branch cm/e15m-spec-v0.3-rope with 'Do NOT merge to main pending review'. The doc is on main, but the branch URL returns 404 unauthenticated, so the branch work is not public.
Gate (3), the token-match oracle runs, was not re-run for v0.3b in that pass.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
labs.learned: Fixing only the reduction improved the error a lot and still failed the bar, because the polynomial was now the dominant error. We kept the bar and changed both the reduction and the polynomials, which met it in the local harness.

explainer.question: Is the pinned sin/cos accurate enough for long contexts, measured against a bar we set before we tested?
explainer.why: Position encoding feeds sin and cos large angles at long context. If those functions are inaccurate there, the spec pins a bad answer exactly.
steps: Write the pass mark first: within 2 ULP of the correctly rounded value.
Build a 60-digit-precision reference for positions up to 8192 on two models.
Score three versions: the original, a better reduction only, and new reduction plus new polynomials.
Report each against the bar.
explainer.headline: 115,198 down to 1.5 ULP
explainer.result: The original was off by up to 115,198 ULP (sin) and 163,969 (cos). A better reduction alone cut the error 55 to 70 times but still missed (up to 2813.5 ULP). The final version reached at most 1.5 ULP on both models. A ULP is the gap between neighbouring numbers.
explainer.meaning: The final version met the bar in our local test. The bar came first, but the final fix was chosen after the second version missed, so it was not itself pre-registered. No cross-machine confirmation was recorded.

labs.title: One flipped bit in the weights: which checks notice?
labs.hard_question: If one bit of an AI model's weights is silently corrupted, can you tell by re-reading its output, or do you need to check the computation itself?
labs.method: Pruned BitNet-2B checkpoint, prompt 'Once upon a time', 64 new tokens, greedy, one host (aefinity-box). Experiment 1 (moat-3): 50 trials (5 no-flip controls, 40 random low-mantissa flips in bits 0-4, 5 forced bit-7 flips); A = text/argmax replay, B = top-5 logit-set match, C = full witness-chain digest match. Experiment 2 (moat-3b): 295 trials stratified by tensor class plus a bit-position sweep; the harness source (commit 1567ee1, header lines 28-30) defines A = generated token ids identical to the clean baseline, B = top-5 logit index set identical at every step, C = witness-chain digest match, which agrees with the write-up's summary tables. The write-up's setup paragraph describes Experiment 2's A and B differently (run completed without error; receipt accepted); the harness code is the authority. Wilson 95% intervals computed for the doc; counts recounted from raw per-trial logs on a second host (recomputation only, not re-inference). Harness commits (14ef1a1, 1567ee1) are public; we did not rebuild them for this summary.

results.claim: Experiment 2 (295 trials): of 247 trials where the output logits changed, text replay (A: same generated token ids) missed 182. The harness source defines A this way; the write-up's setup paragraph describes A differently, but its tables and the code agree.
Experiment 2: the top-5 logit-set check (B, labelled 'top-k / receipt-style' in the write-up's table) missed 82 of the same 247.
results.quote: | top-k / receipt-style check (B) | 82 / 247 | [0.276, 0.393] |

results.claim: The witness digest row is 0 of 247. The document says this is exact by construction, since a digest miss and a C-fail are the same event.
results.quote: | CIS witness digest (C) | 0 / 247 | [0.000, 0.015] |

results.claim: Experiment 1 (50 trials): text replay passed 3 corruptions that the digest caught (trials 16, 25, 47). Top-5 replay also failed on all 3, so its miss count was 0 at this sample size.
results.quote: | A pass AND C fail (text replay misses a corruption the digest catches) | 3 |

results.claim: Null result: 43 flips (37 of 70 SCALE_FFN and 6 of 35 TRIT_FFN trials) left the witness digest identical to the clean baseline. The digest by design stays silent on these, and a byte-level check would flag them.
results.quote: A byte-level integrity check would flag these 43 cases; the CIS digest, by design, does not, because it attests to computation, not storage.

results.claim: The write-up corrected its own original report after the second recount: trial 47 was a bit-7 flip from the random set, not one of the 5 dedicated high-bit control trials.
results.quote: Correction from the second recount: the original report used trial 47 as "the" high-bit example;

caveats: The digest's 0/247 is exact by construction (C is defined as a digest or baseline-output mismatch); the informative numbers are how often A and B miss.

The write-up's setup paragraph describes Experiment 2's A as 'inference completed without error' and B as 'receipt accepted'. The harness source at commit 1567ee1 defines A as identical generated token ids, B as an identical top-5 logit index set and C as a witness-digest match, matching the write-up's tables; we follow the code.
Experiment 1's random flips were low-mantissa bits 0 to 4 only (plus 5 forced bit-7 flips). Flips were chosen by the harness, not an adversary.

B is the top-5 logit-set check in both experiments per the harness source; the write-up's prose calls Experiment 2's B a receipt check. The two experiments' counts are still reported separately, not merged.
In Experiment 1 every method caught all 5 forced high-bit flips. In Experiment 2 the EMBED class (80 trials) was missed by both A and B 80 of 80 times.
Embedding result: EMBED C-fail was 80/80 for the fixed prompt only. The unused-embedding-row case was not tested.
No adversarial (optimised) tampering was tested. No timing claims are made.
One pruned 2B checkpoint, one prompt, one hardware family; second host recomputed counts from logs only. The checkpoint is not linked publicly, so outsiders may not be able to rerun as-is.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
labs.learned: In the larger run, among the 247 trials where the output actually changed, the text-replay column missed 182 and the top-k/receipt-style check missed 82. Some flips (43) changed nothing in the computation. A check on the computation itself is by definition silent only on flips that changed nothing, but that 0/247 is true by construction, so the informative finding is how often the weaker checks miss. Single prompt and model, harness-chosen flips, no adversary.

explainer.question: If one bit of an AI model's weights is silently corrupted, can you tell by re-reading its output, or must you check the computation itself?
explainer.why: Weights are files that can be corrupted or tampered with. Re-reading the answer is the cheap check; checking the computation is the expensive one. We wanted to know how much the cheap one misses.
steps: Take one pruned BitNet-2B model and one prompt, 64 tokens.
Flip single bits in the weights: 50 trials, then 295 trials across tensor classes.
Run three checks on each corrupted run: same text, same top-5 candidates, same computation digest.
Count misses with 95% intervals; recount from raw logs on a second host.
explainer.headline: 182 of 247 missed by text
explainer.result: In the 295-trial run, 247 flips changed the model's output scores. Text replay missed 182 of them and the top-5 check missed 82. The computation digest missed 0, which is true by construction. 43 flips changed nothing in the computation.
explainer.meaning: Comparing output text missed most of the real changes in this test. One model, one prompt, flips chosen by our harness, no adversary. The informative numbers are the two weaker checks' misses, not the digest's built-in 0.
explainer.analogy: Like judging a cake by its look: a swapped ingredient can slip past, but re-baking it step by step shows the difference.

labs.title: Realistic edits to the embedding table, including one hidden row
labs.hard_question: Can a small, realistic edit to a model hide from output checks if the test prompts never touch it?
labs.method: Substitution classes on the bf16 embedding table (vocab 50,256, hidden 2,560) of one pruned BitNet-2B checkpoint: INT8 round-trip (a), 1% magnitude pruning (d), an approximated fine-tune patch (b), and single-row patches of +1 to the row's int8-quantized code (all 2,560 elements of the row move) on rows that the prompts do not read (b') or do read (b''). Global classes used a 20-prompt set; single-row classes used 8 rows x 5 prompts = 40 trials (a 5-prompt subset, rows sampled with a seed-42 PRNG), greedy decode, 64 new tokens. Detectors: A text replay, B top-5 logit-index set, C witness digest; 'detected' means the check differs from baseline. Wilson 95% CIs. Run by us; the harness is not yet published in a public repo.

results.claim: For a single edited embedding row that none of the test prompts read (8 random rows x 5 prompts = 40 trials), text replay and the top-5 check each detected 0 of 40; the witness digest detected 40 of 40.
results.quote: When the row is not exercised by the test prompts, A and B miss it completely (0/40 each in (b')).

results.claim: Control with 8 rows the prompts do read (40 trials): the top-5 check detected 21 of 40 (52.5%, Wilson 37.5-67.1%); text replay detected 11 of 40 (27.5%). Even when rows are read, detection is only partial.
1% magnitude pruning of the whole table (20 prompts): text replay detected 18 of 20 (90.0%, Wilson 69.9-97.2%); the top-5 check and witness digest detected 20 of 20.
In the classes that were run, the witness digest detected every trial. Here 'detected' means the digest differs from baseline; the document reports no false-positive test for it.
results.quote: The witness digest (C) is the only detector of the three that caught every trial in every class tested here

results.claim: UNABLE: substituting a different same-shape checkpoint was found infeasible and not run (no independently trained checkpoint with matching shape was available).
results.quote: ### (c) Different same-shape checkpoint — found infeasible

caveats: Small samples (n=20 or n=40), wide intervals; one checkpoint, one prompt set, embedding table only.
The single-row classes used only a 5-prompt subset of the 20 prompts, and 8 rows; the 40 trials are 8 rows x 5 prompts, not 40 independent rows.
The edit is +1 step of the int8-quantized code on all 2,560 elements of the row, not a bf16 last-bit edit.
The INT8 class changed 96.91% of values (INT8 round-trip: all three detectors 20/20); the document says this does not show A/B would catch a smaller quantization.
The fine-tune class is a labelled approximation (token-bigram nudge), not a real gradient step; the document calls its all-caught result weaker evidence than it looks.

Row choice was a fixed-seed PRNG; the control (b'') drew rows from the prompts' own tokens, a looser selection than (b'). An attacker who knows the test prompts, or a patch confined to rare tokens, was not tested.
The harness is not published, so the experiment cannot be rerun from the repo.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
labs.learned: Output checks are only as good as the prompts you test with. One edited row that no prompt read was missed by text replay and by the top-5 check in 40 of 40 trials, while a check over the computation caught all 40. Even when prompts did read the edited row, those output checks caught only 11 and 21 of 40.

explainer.question: Can a small, realistic edit to a model hide from output checks if the test prompts never touch it?
explainer.why: A realistic model edit may touch only rare words. If your tests never use those words, output checks pass while the model has changed.
steps: Edit the model's word table in realistic ways: INT8 round-trip, 1% pruning, a fine-tune-style patch, single rows.
For single rows: 8 rows the prompts never read, 8 they do read, 5 prompts each (40 trials).
Compare three detectors with the unedited model: text replay, top-5 logits, computation digest.
Report counts with 95% intervals. A same-shape model swap was judged infeasible and not run.

labs.title: Training checkpoints across CPUs and instruction sets
labs.hard_question: If you run the same training job with the same seed on two computers, do you get the same model?

Run by us.

results.quote: **MATCH — cross-machine, not cross-ISA.**

results.claim: The fixed-order C trainer gave identical checkpoint hashes on all five hosts, including one aarch64 phone; a second clean build on one x86_64 host and the phone reproduced the same digests.

CPU only; no GPU host was tested.
The C trainer source is not released.

labs.title: E22: which spec rules does the test vector actually exercise?
labs.hard_question: If we deliberately break one rule of our own spec, does the official test notice?
labs.method: Sixteen single-clause mutations of the C verifier (CIS-2 v0.3b), each built and run against the pinned test vector (a single 4-token prompt on a 135M checkpoint with head_dim = 64) on one host (cm-box1, i5-5200U, gcc 14.2.0), plus unmutated builds at four optimisation levels as positive controls. A clause counts as exercised if breaking it moves the witness digest. Run by us; one machine, one compiler.

results.claim: 12 of 16 mutations moved the digest, 3 did not, 1 was declared skipped (M07, skipped by the leg).
results.quote: **12 of 16 mutations moved the digest. 3 did not. 1 was declared skipped.**

results.claim: The argmax tie-break rule (M15, section 11) is not exercised by this vector because no tie occurs in any of its 16 argmaxes over a 49152-wide fp32 logit vector. The source says the clause is correct and necessary in general and that the vector never reaches the branch.
results.quote: **M15** | **§11 argmax tie-break** | **SAME** | **not exercised**

results.claim: Correction by the authors: the M16 row (attention scale via pinned rsqrt) was a vacuous mutation, because it substituted the function for its own body, so it tested nothing. The first published explanation (head_dim = 64 is a perfect square) was withdrawn as a rationalisation.
results.quote: **VACUOUS MUTATION — see correction below**

results.claim: A rule that can be broken without effect on the digest is untested by this vector, not redundant. This is a statement about the conformance suite, not the spec.
results.quote: A clause that can be broken with no observable effect is not thereby redundant

results.claim: Unmutated builds reproduced the baseline digest at four optimisation levels (O0, O1, O3, Os). Scope is this compiler on this host only.

caveats: One compiler (gcc 14.2.0), one machine (i5-5200U), one 4-token prompt on one 135M checkpoint with head_dim = 64. The source says the silence is a property of this vector, not of the spec.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.

M01 (section 1.3 FTZ/DAZ pin) was revised after the first run by E38, E39 (erratum E-12) and E40 (erratum E-13). Its null is now explained: no denormal arises anywhere in the decode on the two checkpoints tested (E40 counted 562,531,070,920 intermediates, 0 subnormal). The clause is untriggered here, not unnecessary, and there is still no end-to-end necessity witness. The spec guards it separately: section 15 item 4 requires its self-test to pass independently of the digest.
M07 (section 6.1) was skipped, so it is neither a hit nor a miss.

The M16 correction and rsqrt route table were measured on a different host (penguin, Crostini, gcc -O2) than the main matrix. The source says the section 6.1 check rsqrt(64.0) == 0.125 cannot discriminate between implementations. Op-level goldens for rsqrt and the tie-break were added later in cis2-verify (follow-up items 2 and 3 marked done).

The tie-break and the denormal-flush pin are protected only by inputs this vector never contains. labs.title: E29: does the compiler's optimiser change the bits?
labs.hard_question: Does getting identical results mean giving up on fast, optimised code?
labs.method: Every intermediate of the normative decode was dumped from differently compiled builds and compared exactly (sha256 plus a structural diff), with disassembly analysis. Core test: three x86_64 binaries (baseline; target-cpu=native with AVX2 on an i5-10210U; target-cpu=native SSE-only on a Celeron N4020) on SmolLM2-135M and Qwen2.5-0.5B. results.quote: turns out to be **no**: the optimizer may vectorize, and does, and the bits do not move.

results.claim: Ten distinct x86_64 binaries (opt-level 0,1,2,3,s x generic/native) on SmolLM2-135M produced one identical 51,750,154-byte dump, with zero FMA instructions.
results.quote: **Ten distinct binaries. One dump.**

caveats: Core test: two machines (penguin, a ChromeOS Crostini VM, and a bare-metal Celeron box), same glibc, one rustc version (1.98.0, same LLVM). It is not a second-compiler test.

The ten-cell opt-level sweep was SmolLM2-135M only, x86_64, run locally. At opt-level 0 the arithmetic kernels were not vectorised (the 147 ymm instructions there are in tokenizer/allocator code), so the informative cells are opt-level 1/2/3/s with native.
Scope is limited: six prompts, longest context 64 generated tokens, ASCII only; flags outside opt-level, target-cpu, lto, codegen-units and profile-use are untested.

The source later adds an aarch64 half (E31): 20 cells over x86_64 and aarch64 on GitHub-hosted runners, same dump. Same rustc. The earlier 'x86_64 only' caveat applies to the ten-cell sweep, not to the whole document.

labs.hard_question: Do those shrinking tricks survive on real pretrained models, and was our earlier null result even valid?

Run by us.

results.quote: E7's null result was an artifact by construction — retract it.

results.claim: On SmolLM2-135M (fp32), 4-bit per-token activation quantization collapses perplexity from 16.14 to 13,773; a folded rotation sandwich recovers 92.3% of the log-PPL collapse, leaving PPL at 27.11 (still above the 16.14 baseline). On Qwen3-0.6B the recovery was 92.5% (34.23 to 146,845 collapse). Fake-quant is an upper bound on deployable A4.
results.quote: A4 per-token quantization collapses PPL 16.14 → 13,773; a per-linear folded rotation sandwich recovers **92.3%** of the log-PPL collapse (→ 27.11)

labs.title: A compiler setting silently deleted our vector instructions
labs.hard_question: How can code run hundreds of times slower than its parts predict, with no error and correct output?
labs.method: Counted the vector instructions in the binary actually shipped (objdump census of a preserved copy), then rebuilt with a custom hard-float target and measured ticks/token on the Dell Inspiron 15 (i5-5200U, bare metal, no OS). A pre-registered root-cause prediction was scored. Run by us.

results.claim: Hand-written AVX2 kernels compiled to zero vector instructions; the binary ran 217 to 258 times slower than the hard-float rebuild (soft-float 1.65-1.67e9 vs hard-float 6.48-7.59e6 ticks/token).
results.quote: Our hand-written AVX2 kernels compiled to zero vector instructions, and the resulting binary ran 217–258× slower than it should have.

results.claim: Instruction census of the shipped (preserved, bit-identical) soft-float binary: no xmm, ymm or vfmadd instructions.
results.quote: census: xmm=0 ymm=0 vfmadd=0

caveats: One machine (Dell Inspiron 15, i5-5200U, bare metal, no OS); 217 to 258 times is the ratio of soft-float to hard-float ticks/token on that machine, derived from ranges (1.65e9/7.59e6 to 1.67e9/6.48e6), not a controlled benchmark.
A debugging post-mortem tied to Rust's stock x86_64-unknown-uefi target (+soft-float).
The first census (v1) was itself wrong because a concurrent rebuild overwrote the artifact; it was re-run on a preserved bit-identical copy and the log superseded. Conclusion unchanged.
A pre-registered root-cause prediction was also scored, in an analysis that covers the held-back operating-system comparison; we do not link that analysis while the comparison is held back.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
labs.learned: Trust the binary you ship, not the annotation you wrote. Nothing failed and nothing warned; only counting instructions in the artifact exposed it. A mechanical check (assert nonzero ymm/vfmadd count in CI) is the fix, not a benchmark.

labs.title: E-S1: how far can a ternary 2B model be compressed without loss?

labs.method: Census and lossless coding (rANS, xz, zstd) of all 2,084,044,800 weights in the 210 body tensors of the BitNet-b1.58-2B engine model file aegis_pruned_model.safetensors, with a byte-exact round trip, on one Dell i5-5200U. Counts and byte sizes only. Run by us.

results.claim: The best of the lossless coders tested (zstd -19 on packed bytes) reached 1.532 bits per weight, 399,113,010 bytes, against 2.000 bits per weight for the engine's current packing.

Counts and byte sizes only. Coding speed was not measured.
Run by us; no unaffiliated reproduction.
